body_ar:
الصفات التي أثبتها الله لنفسه أو أثبتها له رسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم يجب إثباتها؛ لكن بغير تشبيه ولا تأويل ولا تعطيل.
إثبات الصفات مشروط بعدم التكييف والتمثيل والتحريف والتأويل
قال: [من غير ما تكييف أو تمثيل له ولا تحريف أو تأويل] ......
معنى التحريف:
(ولا تحريف): أي: لا تحرف هذه النصوص، والمعنى: ولا تنقل عن دلالتها الأصلية، بل تترك على دلالتها، وتحريف النص معناه: وضعه في غير موضعه، كما قال تعالى:  يُحَرِّفُونَ الْكَلِمَ عَنْ مَوَاضِعِه  [النساء:46] . وأصله تحريف القلم، أي: الميل به عن أن يكون عمودياً، وأن يكون في كتابته أفقياً، فتعطيل إحدى سني القلم عن الأخرى هو تحريف، وتحريف الكلام معناه: نقله وبتره وتحويله من موضعه إلى موضع آخر، فمثلاً الكلام الذي جاء في الثناء على الله من الوجه والعينين واليدين ينقله بعض الناس إلى أن يجعله عيباً ونقصاً، وهذا تحريف للكلم عن مواضعه، فالله عز وجل أتى به ثناءً على نفسه، فكيف ينقل ويجعل نقصاً وعيباً؟ هذا تحريف واضح...
body_en:
*[Site synopsis]* The attributes that God has affirmed of Himself, or that His Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, has affirmed of Him, must be affirmed — but without likening Him to creation, without interpretation and without stripping Him of them.

## The affirmation of the attributes is conditional upon there being no asking how, no comparison, no distortion and no interpretation

He said: *[without any asking how or comparison; and there is for Him no distortion or interpretation.]* ......

## The meaning of distortion

"And no distortion": that is, do not distort these texts — the meaning being, do not shift them away from what they originally signify; rather leave them upon what they signify. Distorting a text means putting it somewhere other than its own place, as He, exalted is He, said: {they distort words from their places} (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:46). Its origin is the tilting of the pen — that is, inclining it away from being upright, so that in its writing it lies flat; disabling one of the pen's two nib-edges with respect to the other is distortion. And distorting speech means shifting it, cutting it short and moving it from its place to another place.

So, for example, the words that have come in praise of God concerning the face, the two eyes and the two hands: some people shift them so as to make of them a fault and a deficiency. This is distorting the words from their places. God, mighty and majestic, brought them as praise of Himself — so how is it to be shifted and made a deficiency and a fault? This is plain distortion …

flags.arabic: الفقرة الافتتاحية مقابل ما بعد العنوان الفرعي
flags.context: the synopsis paragraph against the transcribed commentary
options: mark the synopsis as the site's own and the remainder as the Sheikh's words
present the whole record as the Sheikh's words
flags.note: The record has two authors. The opening paragraph is a synopsis written by the site, speaking about the lesson in the third person; everything from the section heading onward is the lecturer's own words as transcribed, together with the quoted lines of the versified base text, which are his teacher's. Three voices in all, and the site must keep them apart.

flags.arabic: قال شيخنا حفظه الله في منظومته في الأسماء والصفات
flags.context: the formula introducing each quoted line of the versified base text in this series
options: read 'our Sheikh' as the author of the versification, the lecturer's own teacher
read it as Sheikh al-Dedew quoting his own verse
flags.note: Record 734 of this series settles the referent in a way the creed run (IDs 707-721) did not: it has 'قال شيخنا حفظه الله في منظومته في الأسماء والصفات' — 'OUR Sheikh, may God preserve him, said in his versification on the names and attributes'. The first-person plural possessive makes the author the lecturer's own teacher, living at the time of the lesson, and the base text a versification devoted specifically to the divine names and attributes. Elsewhere in the series the shorter 'قال الشيخ' and 'يقول الشيخ' are used for the same person. The author is nowhere named. Note that this is a different base text from the versified creed expounded in records 707-721, which record 719 identifies as a versification of the Mukhtaṣar of Khalil.

flags.arabic: الكلام الذي جاء في الثناء على الله من الوجه والعينين واليدين ينقله بعض الناس إلى أن يجعله عيباً ونقصاً
options: render the argument exactly and attribute it to him, flagging that it takes a side
render it as a neutral account of a disagreement
flags.note: The most doctrinally loaded passage in the series so far, and it is in the lecturer's own voice. He treats the scriptural language of the face, the two eyes and the two hands as praise of God, and characterises the reading of it as a fault or deficiency as a distortion of scripture. That is a position in the long dispute between the schools over the divine attributes, and the Sheikh is being presented in English as holding it. Two cautions. First, the served text does not say who 'some people' are, and no group has been named in the English. Second, the record breaks off before interpretation (taʾwīl) is discussed at all — which is the term under which the schools he is arguing against would describe their own procedure — so his position as served is incomplete. Style guide sections 10 and 12 both apply, and the full text should be obtained before this is published.

flags.context: the four terms in the section heading and the quoted verse
options: asking how, comparison, distortion and interpretation
modality, likening, alteration and figurative reading
flags.note: Four technical terms, none of them in the glossary, and the whole record is a commentary on them. 'تكييف' is asking after the manner or 'how' of a divine attribute — a noun English does not have, hence the gerund phrase. 'تمثيل' is the assertion of a like. 'تحريف' is the shifting of a text from its place, which the lecturer glosses at length and which 'distortion' carries. 'تأويل' is fixed in the glossary as 'interpretation' in the Qur'anic-exegesis sense, but here it is the fourth member of a list of things rejected, which is a sharper and more polemical use than the glossary's neutral entry contemplates. These four should be fixed corpus-wide, and the glossary entry for taʾwīl should be revisited: a term that is neutral in one register and an accusation in another cannot carry a single fixed rendering without a note.

flags.arabic: وأصله تحريف القلم ... فتعطيل إحدى سني القلم عن الأخرى هو تحريف
options: the tilting of the pen … disabling one of the pen's two nib-edges with respect to the other
the slanting of the pen … taking one of the pen's two points out of use
the angling of the reed … neglecting one of its two edges
flags.note: A concrete image from the calligrapher's craft: the reed pen is cut to a broad, obliquely angled nib, and holding it tilted so that only one edge of the cut bears on the page changes the letter. The whole argument about scripture is built on it — a text held at the wrong angle writes a different word. 'سنّ' is a tooth and hence the point or edge of a nib; 'nib-edge' has been used to keep the image concrete without inventing a term. Note that 'تعطيل', here used of a pen, is the same word used for stripping God of His attributes elsewhere in the series, and the English cannot keep the echo.

options: it is obligatory (wājib) to affirm them
flags.note: A borderline case for style guide section 8. The subject of the ruling is an act of a responsible person — affirming — so the legal reading is available and 'obligatory (wājib)' would be defensible. But the sentence is about what must be held true of God, which is nearer to rational necessity than to a ruling on conduct, and the source gives no other ruling term anywhere in the record. 'Must be affirmed' has been chosen because it does not decide between the two, where 'obligatory (wājib)' would assert the legal reading. The sentence is in any case the site's and not the Sheikh's.

translator_notes: One of a run of fourteen records, IDs 734-747, the series 'The Names and Attributes', all built to the same template and all excerpts. Each carries a site-written synopsis, then a section heading, then the opening formula and the first lines of a lesson, and then breaks off on an ellipsis; the full text sits behind a .doc download in the /medias/doc/esmawesivat-* series, numbered 1 to 14 in the same order as the IDs. None of the SEF aliases in this run carries a timestamp, so no upload date can be read from them.

The source's final line, 'تحميل المادة' ('download the material'), is the label of a download link in the page furniture, not part of the text. It is recorded as source_download_link and omitted from body_ar and body_en.
Qur'anic renderings here are interpretive and are not a substitute for the Arabic.

The record is broken twice: six dots stand where the commentary on the quoted verse should begin, and the text breaks off again at the end. The section heading of the lost portion names all four terms; only the third is expounded in what survives.
The first section heading is served without a colon, unlike the second and unlike the rest of this series; reproduced as served.
The English breaks the surviving commentary into two paragraphs where the source runs on, separating the definition from the example. No word has been added or removed.
